role: Author source-reading supplement; not an independent scientific review

claims.claim: YwhB from B. subtilis catalyzes several tested enol/dienol ketonizations in vitro. The paper explicitly leaves its biological function unresolved and identifies no genomic context establishing a pathway.
claims.source_locator: Abstract; introduction paragraph on YwhB; S20 discussion
claims.limitations: Do not promote this adjacent activity to experimental evidence for a complete native B. subtilis catechol pathway or infer a particular strain/current protein accession from this paper alone.

claims.claim: P1A and R11A YwhB mutants were overproduced in E. coli BL21(DE3)pLysS and purified to more than 95% homogeneity by the reported SDS-PAGE assessment. Their DNA sequences and expected protein masses were checked.
claims.limitations: Exact mutagenesis, expression, purification and mass-spectral procedures are relegated to unread supporting information. Do not apply the reported mutant purification threshold to every wild-type preparation without its cited prior protocol.

claims.claim: The main report interprets mutant mass spectra as showing the expected products without a retained initiating methionine blocking the first catalytic residue. Mutant labels use processed enzyme positions P1A and R11A.
claims.limitations: Mass spectra themselves and full construct sequences were unavailable. Do not conflate processed Pro-1 with a residue number in an unverified current accession, or infer tag state and all termini.

claims.claim: Steady-state assays used 20 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.3, at 23°C, with spectrophotometric monitoring and nonlinear regression. Table errors are standard deviations.
claims.limitations: The authors could not reach saturation for some substrates and identify the resulting fitted kcat values as estimates. No individual affected rows are explicitly marked; retain that general limitation.

claims.claim: For compound 2→1, YwhB performs 1,3 ketonization of 2-hydroxymuconate to the β,γ-unsaturated keto tautomer, with kcat 10±1 s−1 and Km 76±17 µM under the assay conditions.
claims.source_locator: Scheme 1 (F3); Table 1 row 1 / inline nihms62730t1.jpg; S14
claims.limitations: This 2→1 chemistry is distinct from the pathway-directed 2→3 1,5 ketonization. Paper compound numbers and drawings do not independently resolve disputed modern cross-reference stereoisomers.

claims.claim: YwhB also catalyzes compound 2→3, the 1,5 ketonization, with kcat 26.0±1.4 s−1 and Km 940±70 µM; its catalytic efficiency is 2.8±0.2 × 10^4 M−1 s−1.
claims.source_locator: Table 1 row 6 / inline nihms62730t6.jpg; S5; S14
claims.limitations: The 2→1 catalytic efficiency is higher even though its kcat is lower. Do not describe efficiency preference as a larger turnover number or as a proven physiological role.

claims.claim: YwhB converts HPD (compound 5) to 2-oxo-4-pentenoate (4) by 1,3 ketonization: kcat 112±14 s−1, Km 243±42 µM and kcat/Km 4.6±0.8 × 10^5 M−1 s−1.
claims.source_locator: Scheme 1; Table 1 row 2; Table 2; inline nihms62730t2.jpg and nihms62730f9.jpg
claims.limitations: These data describe ketonization, not hydration. They do not establish that this reaction supplies native B. subtilis catechol catabolism.

claims.claim: YwhB catalyzes 1,3 ketonization of phenylenolpyruvate (7), p-hydroxyphenylenolpyruvate (8) and the seven-carbon dicarboxylate dienol (11); efficiencies differ substantially across these analogues.
claims.limitations: These available synthetic test substrates were chosen for mechanistic study. Broad in-vitro acceptance is not proof of physiological substrate availability or pathway membership.

claims.claim: Only the six-carbon diacid 2 yielded a measurable YwhB 1,5 ketonization rate among the tested dienols. Corresponding α,β-keto formation from 5 and 11 was too close to nonenzymatic rates to measure reliably.
claims.limitations: Do not replace a rate-resolution limit with an absolute statement of zero possible activity under all conditions. Compounds 7 and 8 are enols, not additional dienol tests.

claims.claim: P1A and R11A eliminate detectable 2→1 and 2→3 activities under the reported assays. Both retain reduced ketonization of HPD and phenylenolpyruvate; Arg-11 replacement has the larger effect.
claims.limitations: This implicates both residues in activity. The detailed general-base, carbanion-stabilization and substrate-binding roles remain mechanistic interpretations rather than direct observations of proton trajectories or bound substrates.

claims.claim: Table 2 reports HPD Km values of 243±42 µM for wild-type YwhB and 378±100 µM for P1A, an approximately 1.56-fold increase. S15 instead calls it a 1.6-fold decrease.
claims.source_locator: Table 2, wild-type and P1A rows; S15
claims.limitations: Retain the explicit table numbers and flag the contradictory prose. The roughly 70-fold loss of catalytic efficiency agrees with the table; do not silently propagate the erroneous direction.

claims.claim: Products generated in D2O were trapped by borohydride reduction and converted through ozonolysis and malic-enzyme treatment to labeled malate. Partial proton NMR spectra were used to assign isotope-dependent stereochemistry.
claims.limitations: The spectra concern downstream analytical derivatives. Borohydride reduction is stereorandom at the new hydroxyl center, and malic enzyme removes one malate diastereomer before analysis.

claims.claim: Ketonization of HPD (5) by YwhB in D2O favors (3R)-[3-2H]-2-oxo-4-pentenoate (4) by approximately 4.4:1, inferred from the derivatized malate NMR signals.
claims.source_locator: S8; S17; Scheme 4 (F6); Figure 1B (F1); Table 4 row 1
claims.limitations: This is a product mixture, not exclusive stereospecificity. The C-3 R/S label depends on deuterium substitution; ordinary unlabeled compound 4 has no corresponding C-3 stereocenter.

claims.claim: Phenylenolpyruvate (7) ketonization in D2O favors (3R)-[3-2H]-phenylpyruvate (9) by approximately 3:1 in the reported derivatization/NMR analysis.
claims.source_locator: S6–S7; S16; Scheme 3 (F5); Figure 1A (F1); Table 4 row 2
claims.limitations: This partial stereoselectivity belongs to the labeled product and assay conditions. It is not proof of an absolute stereochemical identity for the ordinary unlabeled metabolite.

claims.claim: YwhB ketonization of diacid 2 to compound 1 in D2O favors (3S)-[3-2H]-2-oxo-4-hexenedioate by approximately 8:1, opposite to the favored C-3 configuration for the tested monoacids.
claims.source_locator: S9–S10; S18; Scheme 5 (F7); Figure 2A (F2); Table 4 row 4
claims.limitations: This does not establish 2→3 stereochemistry or modern alkene E/Z identity. A proposed diacid physiological substrate is an author hypothesis, not a demonstrated biological function.

claims.claim: Incubating diacid 2 with 4-OT in D2O yielded approximately equal C-3 isotope stereoisomers of keto compound 1. The analysis was repeated with the same result.
claims.limitations: The result questions a 4-OT-catalyzed 1,3 step but does not prove its absence. S20 explicitly retains an alternative involving two binding orientations and calls for direct rate-acceleration evidence.

claims.claim: The YwhB diacid reaction proceeded for 1 min before NaBH4 addition and then 1 h before workup. In the 4-OT comparator, enzyme and NaBH4 were added together and the mixtures stood overnight.
claims.limitations: The main paper describes otherwise comparable conditions, but enzyme amounts and trapping/incubation timing differ. Preserve the actual protocols rather than asserting identical preparations.

claims.claim: After trapping the YwhB diacid reaction, the isolated material contained about 26 mg of reduced compound 1 and 11 mg of reduced compound 3. The 4-OT experiment recovered these reduced products in an approximate 1:2 ratio.
claims.limitations: These are isolation/NMR composition observations under different trapping protocols, not steady-state branching fluxes, equilibrium constants or native intracellular product ratios.

claims.claim: Opposite labeled C-3 preferences for monoacids and diacid 2 motivate different substrate orientations involving Arg-11. Pro-1 general-base chemistry and altered charge stabilization are proposed explanations for the mutant effects.
claims.limitations: No ligand-bound YwhB structure or direct binding-orientation measurement is presented. Do not encode a particular contact, proton face or physiological diacid as experimentally demonstrated.

claims.claim: The introduction describes YwhB as a hexamer of 61-residue subunits and cites prior structural literature. This study does not newly determine its native oligomerization.
claims.limitations: Do not label hexamer assembly as a fresh 2007 measurement or use it as exact sequence/assembly evidence for another tautomerase such as XylH or PraC.

claims.claim: The cited 4-OT 2→3 kinetic comparator is kcat 3500 s−1 and Km 180 µM. S14 attributes these values to reference 13, rather than measuring them anew in the YwhB kinetic table.
claims.limitations: Keep the prior-source attribution and preparation distinction. Table 4 also imports selected 4-OT stereochemical ratios from references 7, 13 and 31; only its 2→1 racemate comparator is newly analyzed here.

claims.claim: The authors propose that the pathway role of 4-OT may be primarily 2→3 1,5 ketonization, with keto compound 1 interconverting chemically with enol 2. They present this as a revised possibility requiring kinetic discrimination.
claims.limitations: Do not treat this as conclusive proof that 4-OT never accelerates 1↔2. It does distinguish YwhB’s measured adjacent 2→1 reaction from the formal 2→3 pathway reaction.
